fatal_errors: The proposed Inconel 718 friction-stir-processing intervention does not reconstruct the mechanically alloyed HEA powder, SPS electrode consolidation, and electrospark-deposition route of the target.
It claims improved wear and corrosion performance in aggressive environments even though the target performed no corrosion or service-environment testing.

The sole citation concerns generic friction-stir surface processing and a copper-composite context; it does not substantiate FSP of Inconel 718, compressive residual stress, hot-crack suppression, or the claimed corrosion improvement.
The initial state conflates a damaged component with one already subjected to a cracking-prone fusion-weld repair and does not clearly explain how FSP restores missing material or repairs the damage.
Processing and service boundaries are under-specified: traverse speed, tool geometry, force, depth, temperature limits, corrosive medium, temperature, load, and exposure duration are absent.
explanation: The hypothesis recognizes the broad need for a lower-heat surface intervention and proposes a potentially plausible solid-state alternative with relevant untreated and fusion-welded controls. Its experiment includes useful characterization and a statistically framed falsification rule. Nevertheless, it has essentially no agreement with the target materials, SPS and ESD processing windows, layer-count comparison, multiphase coating mechanism, or measured densification, porosity, hardness, and coating-defect outcomes. Its central service-performance and hot-cracking claims extend well beyond the cited evidence. The experiment is directionally discriminating but combines several degradation modes, lacks quantitative effect thresholds, and does not adequately separate repair capability from surface-property modification.
